title: Guru Angad: humility
hookLine: the second Guru's light: the humble disciple who became the Guru
tomorrow: the emperor came to see the Guru. where did he have to sit?

cards: Steam, the clank of steel trays, and the smell of rice cooking slowly in milk. Simran is at the gurdwara langar on dish duty, sleeves pushed up, hands red from hot water, and she's been at it for hours.
Up front, people are thanking the cooks. Nobody is thanking the sink. She sends you a photo of a mountain of pots.
So how does a disciple become the Guru? Not by a contest. By the work nobody photographs.

teach.b: Tradition remembers a man named Lehna, who came to Guru Nanak at Kartarpur and stayed to serve.

The stories told about him are small and muddy: carrying a bundle of wet grass on his head, in his good clothes, because it needed carrying; doing the jobs others in the household thought beneath them.
When the time came, Guru Nanak placed the Guruship on Lehna and named him Angad. A hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib by the bards Satta and Balvand says it simply.
In paraphrase: the light was the same, the way was the same; only the body changed. That same hymn keeps a smell and a taste.
It names Guru Angad's wife, Mata Khivi, a good woman who gave shade to all like a leafy tree, and in her langar, kheer, rice pudding, rich with ghee.
One to tell a friend tonight: the Sikh scripture remembers a woman by the rice pudding she served.
And Guru Nanak gives the word for what Lehna had, in Asa di Var: sweetness and humility are the essence of every virtue. Not thinking little of yourself.
Sweetness, and a low place, chosen. Simran keeps scrubbing. A kid from the youth group picks up a towel beside her and doesn't say a word.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Angad as the disciple Lehna who served Guru Nanak; Sikhs serve in the langar by cooking, serving and washing up, and the scrubbing of dishes is a common first seva for young people.

o: Guru Nanak's eldest son, who inherited his father's seat
the second Guru, the disciple who served without being seen
a warrior Guru who built the first Sikh fort in Punjab

games.q: the second Guru — tap the pairs.
p: the disciple who carried the wet grass
the name Guru Nanak gave him
the bards: only the body changed

s: Guru Nanak passed the Guruship to one of his sons
he placed it on Lehna, his disciple, and named him Angad.
the Guru Granth Sahib names Mata Khivi and her langar
Satta and Balvand's hymn remembers her shade and her kheer.
humility means thinking you're worth very little
Guru Nanak pairs it with sweetness: a low place, chosen, not self-contempt.

games.q: your team needs a new captain. one player loudly says he deserves it; another quietly sets up the cones before every practice. what does Lehna's story point to?
o: the loud one; a captain has to want it and say so.
the one setting up cones; the unseen work counts.
neither; take a vote so it's fair to everyone.
games.why: Lehna didn't campaign. he carried the wet grass. Guru Nanak placed the Guruship on the one doing the unseen work.

practice: If there's a cup, a dish or a counter near you, wash or wipe it slowly by hand, one someone else would otherwise have to do. Feel the warmth of the water and notice the smell of the soap.
Don't mention it to anyone afterward; let it stay quiet.

wordCard.voice: Guru Angad: the second Guru, once Lehna, the disciple who did the work nobody saw. Same light, a new body.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nimrata, humility; a low place, chosen.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: humility, sweetness and a low place, chosen. Same light, new hands, old pots.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 966-967 (Ramkali ki Var, Satta and Balvand: the same light, the same way, only the body changed; Mata Khivi's shade and her langar of kheer with ghee), paraphrased
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470 (Asa di Var, salok Mahalla 1, 'mithat neevee Nanaka gun changiaaeeaa tat': sweetness and humility, the essence of virtue), paraphrased
Sikh tradition: the sakhis of Bhai Lehna's service at Kartarpur (the bundle of wet grass)
